blocks.text: A 52-year-old man with viral hepatitis has a blood test showing alanine aminotransferase (ALT) at several times the upper reference limit. ALT is an enzyme that sits inside liver cells, so its appearance in blood tells you that hepatocytes are leaking. But what does ALT actually do inside the cell, and why does a vitamin B6 derivative sit in its active site?

blocks.markdown:
Every day an adult breaks down protein and amino acids that exceed the body's needs. Amino acids cannot be stored, and their amino group (-NH2) cannot simply be burned for energy. Catabolism therefore has two separate jobs: (1) **remove the nitrogen** and carry it safely to the liver for disposal, and (2) **burn or convert the carbon skeleton** that remains. Free ammonia (NH3, present mostly as ammonium, NH4+, at physiological pH) is toxic to the brain, so nitrogen is always moved around attached to carrier molecules rather than as free ammonium.

The first step for most amino acids is **transamination**: the amino group is not released but is transferred to a keto acid. Transamination is freely reversible, so it moves nitrogen between molecules without any net loss of nitrogen from the body. Net removal needs a second step, **oxidative deamination**, described below.

blocks.title: Aminotransferase and pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)
blocks.text: An aminotransferase (transaminase) is an enzyme that transfers the alpha-amino group from an amino acid to the alpha-carbon of a keto acid. The amino acid becomes a keto acid and the keto acid becomes an amino acid. Every aminotransferase uses pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP), the active form of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine), as its covalently bound coenzyme. The keto acid acceptor is usually alpha-ketoglutarate, which becomes glutamate.

blocks.caption: General transamination reaction; the equilibrium constant is close to 1, so the reaction runs in either direction depending on the concentrations of reactants.

blocks.markdown:
**How PLP works (the ping-pong mechanism).** In the resting enzyme the aldehyde group of PLP is joined to the side-chain amino group of an active-site lysine through a Schiff base (an imine, C=N). When the substrate amino acid binds, its alpha-amino group displaces the lysine and forms a new Schiff base with PLP. Electrons are then shifted through the ring of PLP, which acts as an electron sink, and the Schiff base is hydrolysed. The keto acid product leaves and the amino group stays behind on the coenzyme, which is now **pyridoxamine phosphate (PMP)**. The second substrate, alpha-ketoglutarate, then enters, takes the amino group from PMP (the reverse sequence), and leaves as glutamate, regenerating PLP. Because the first product leaves before the second substrate enters, this is called a ping-pong mechanism.

The two aminotransferases measured clinically are **ALT** (alanine + alpha-ketoglutarate gives pyruvate + glutamate; mainly cytosolic and most concentrated in liver) and **AST** (aspartate + alpha-ketoglutarate gives oxaloacetate + glutamate; found in liver, heart, skeletal muscle and kidney, in both cytosol and mitochondria).

blocks.title: Following one amino group through AST
blocks.prompt: Aspartate (4 carbons, one amino group) is acted on by aspartate aminotransferase (AST) in the presence of alpha-ketoglutarate. Identify the products, say what happens to the amino group, and state what the net change in total body nitrogen is.

steps.text: Write the substrates: the amino acid is aspartate and the keto acid acceptor is alpha-ketoglutarate (5 carbons).
Aspartate loses its alpha-amino group and becomes the keto acid with the same carbon skeleton, which is oxaloacetate (4 carbons).
The amino group is carried temporarily by PLP, which becomes PMP, and is then handed to alpha-ketoglutarate, which becomes glutamate (5 carbons, now bearing the amino group).
Count nitrogen: one amino group enters on aspartate and one leaves on glutamate. Nitrogen has only moved from one carbon skeleton to another.

blocks.answer: Products are oxaloacetate and glutamate. The amino group is transferred, not removed, so total nitrogen in the body is unchanged. Glutamate is now the nitrogen collector.

blocks.markdown:
**Why glutamate is the hub.** Most aminotransferases funnel amino groups onto alpha-ketoglutarate to make glutamate. In the liver, glutamate is taken into mitochondria and undergoes **oxidative deamination** by **glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH)**, which releases the nitrogen as free ammonium and regenerates alpha-ketoglutarate:

glutamate + NAD+ (or NADP+) + H2O gives alpha-ketoglutarate + NH4+ + NADH (or NADPH).

The ammonium released here is the substrate of the urea cycle, which is taught in the next unit. Together, transamination (collecting nitrogen into glutamate) followed by GDH (releasing it) is called **transdeamination**. Lysine and threonine are unusual in that most of their nitrogen does not pass through a simple transamination, but you do not need to learn this exception for this course.

rows: A glucogenic fragment (for example fumarate, succinyl-CoA or pyruvate) plus acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate
Alanine, aspartate, glutamate, valine, serine, glycine and most others
Pyruvate or a citric acid cycle intermediate (alpha-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, fumarate, oxaloacetate)
blocks.caption: Fate of the carbon skeleton. The classification of a few amino acids (for example threonine) differs between textbooks and is not examined here.

blocks.markdown: **Glucogenic versus ketogenic.** An amino acid is **glucogenic** if its carbon skeleton is converted to pyruvate or to a citric acid cycle intermediate. These can be turned into oxaloacetate and then into glucose by gluconeogenesis, giving a *net* gain of carbon for glucose. An amino acid is **ketogenic** if it is converted to acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate. Acetyl-CoA cannot be converted to a net amount of glucose in mammals: when its two carbons enter the citric acid cycle, two carbons leave as CO2, so there is no net gain of oxaloacetate. Instead, acetyl-CoA and acetoacetate are used for ketone bodies and fatty acids. Leucine and lysine are the only purely ketogenic amino acids.

blocks.title: Classifying an amino acid from its breakdown products
blocks.prompt: Tyrosine is degraded to fumarate and acetoacetate. Classify tyrosine, and decide whether tyrosine carbon can contribute to blood glucose during fasting.

steps.text: Sort each product. Fumarate is an intermediate of the citric acid cycle, so it can be converted to oxaloacetate and then to glucose: this fragment is glucogenic.
Acetoacetate is a ketone body that is converted to acetyl-CoA: this fragment is ketogenic.
An amino acid yielding both types of fragment is classed as both glucogenic and ketogenic.
For glucose: only the fumarate-derived carbons can contribute net carbon. The acetoacetate carbons cannot, because they enter as acetyl-CoA.

blocks.answer: Tyrosine is both glucogenic (via fumarate) and ketogenic (via acetoacetate); only part of its carbon skeleton can become glucose.

blocks.markdown:
**Moving ammonia from tissues to the liver.** Peripheral tissues, especially skeletal muscle, break down amino acids and generate amino nitrogen that has to reach the liver. It travels in two non-toxic forms:

- **Glutamine** is made in muscle, brain and many other tissues from glutamate and ammonium by **glutamine synthetase**, which uses ATP: glutamate + NH4+ + ATP gives glutamine + ADP + Pi. Glutamine carries **two** nitrogens (the alpha-amino group and the amide group), is neutral and non-toxic, and travels in blood. In the liver (and in the kidney) **glutaminase** hydrolyses it back to glutamate and NH4+.
- **Alanine** is made in muscle when glutamate (carrying nitrogen) transaminates with pyruvate from glycolysis, using ALT. Alanine carries **one** nitrogen. In the liver the reverse ALT reaction regenerates pyruvate and glutamate; the pyruvate can be made into glucose, which returns to muscle. This loop is the **glucose-alanine cycle**.

rows: Pyruvate can be used for gluconeogenesis
blocks.caption: Two carrier systems for amino nitrogen travelling from peripheral tissues to the liver.

blocks.title: Nitrogen accounting through the alanine route
blocks.prompt: Muscle exports 8 mmol of alanine to the liver in a given period. How much free ammonium can the liver release from this alanine, and how much pyruvate is produced?

steps.text: In the liver, ALT transfers the alanine amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate, giving pyruvate and glutamate in a 1:1 ratio with alanine. So 8 mmol alanine gives 8 mmol pyruvate and 8 mmol glutamate.
Glutamate dehydrogenase removes one NH4+ per glutamate. So 8 mmol glutamate gives 8 mmol NH4+ and regenerates 8 mmol alpha-ketoglutarate.
Summarise: one nitrogen per alanine means the NH4+ yield equals the alanine amount.

blocks.answer: 8 mmol NH4+ (delivered to the urea cycle) and 8 mmol pyruvate, which can be used for gluconeogenesis.

blocks.title: Do not confuse transamination with deamination
blocks.text: Transamination only swaps an amino group between molecules, so ammonium is not produced and total nitrogen is unchanged. Ammonium is released only by deamination (mainly glutamate dehydrogenase) or hydrolysis (glutaminase). Also remember that an enzyme that needs PLP will be impaired by vitamin B6 deficiency, such as that caused by the drug isoniazid, so transamination is the reaction class that depends on this vitamin.

points: Aminotransferases use PLP and a ping-pong mechanism (PLP to PMP and back) to move amino groups onto alpha-ketoglutarate, making glutamate.
Glutamate dehydrogenase in liver mitochondria releases NH4+ from glutamate, regenerating alpha-ketoglutarate.
Leucine and lysine are purely ketogenic; isoleucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan are both; the rest are glucogenic.
Muscle sends nitrogen to the liver as glutamine (via glutamine synthetase) and as alanine (glucose-alanine cycle).

questions.stem: A patient treated with isoniazid for tuberculosis is also given pyridoxine (vitamin B6) supplements. Which type of reaction most directly depends on the active form of this vitamin?

options.text: Transfer of amino groups between amino acids and keto acids
Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA
Transfer of one-carbon units in nucleotide synthesis

questions.correctOptionText: Transfer of amino groups between amino acids and keto acids

distractorRationale.a: Correct: PLP is the coenzyme of every aminotransferase.
distractorRationale.b: Pyruvate dehydrogenase uses thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoate, FAD, NAD+ and CoA, not PLP.

questions.explanation: The active form of vitamin B6 is pyridoxal phosphate, which is the coenzyme of all aminotransferases. It forms a Schiff base with the substrate amino acid and carries the amino group as pyridoxamine phosphate before handing it to a keto acid. The other reactions listed depend on thiamine, biotin and folate-derived cofactors.

questions.stem: A liver biopsy sample is incubated with aspartate and alpha-ketoglutarate. Aspartate aminotransferase is active. Which pair of products forms?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: aspartate loses its amino group to become oxaloacetate; alpha-ketoglutarate gains it to become glutamate.
distractorRationale.b: Pyruvate is the keto acid of alanine (the ALT reaction), not aspartate.
distractorRationale.c: Transamination does not release free ammonium; the amino group is transferred.
distractorRationale.d: Fumarate is not a product, and glutamine needs glutamine synthetase and ATP.

questions.explanation: Each amino acid is converted to the keto acid with the same carbon skeleton, and aspartate corresponds to oxaloacetate. The acceptor alpha-ketoglutarate becomes glutamate. No free ammonium appears because transamination only moves the amino group.

questions.stem: A dietitian is designing a metabolic study and needs an amino acid that cannot supply any net carbon for glucose synthesis. Which amino acid should she choose?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: leucine is purely ketogenic and is degraded to acetyl-CoA and acetoacetate.
distractorRationale.b: Alanine is converted to pyruvate and is glucogenic.
distractorRationale.c: Aspartate is converted to oxaloacetate and is glucogenic.
distractorRationale.d: Glutamate is converted to alpha-ketoglutarate and is glucogenic.

questions.explanation: Leucine (with lysine) is purely ketogenic: its carbons end up as acetyl-CoA and acetoacetate. Acetyl-CoA cannot give a net gain of oxaloacetate because two carbons are lost as CO2 per turn of the citric acid cycle. The other three amino acids enter as pyruvate or citric acid cycle intermediates and are glucogenic.

questions.stem: During a prolonged mountain trek, skeletal muscle breaks down protein. Which pair of molecules is the main way this muscle returns amino nitrogen to the liver without raising free ammonium in blood?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: alanine (glucose-alanine cycle) and glutamine are the main nitrogen carriers from muscle.
distractorRationale.b: Aspartate and arginine are urea cycle participants within the liver, not major muscle export carriers.
distractorRationale.c: Free ammonium is toxic and is not the usual transport form; urea is made in the liver, not muscle.
distractorRationale.d: Pyruvate and oxaloacetate are keto acids and carry carbon, not amino nitrogen.

questions.explanation: Muscle makes alanine by transamination of pyruvate and glutamine by glutamine synthetase, then exports both to the blood. This keeps free ammonium low. The liver then converts both back to glutamate and ammonium for the urea cycle.

questions.stem: In hepatocyte mitochondria, glutamate is converted to alpha-ketoglutarate with release of free ammonium and generation of NADH or NADPH. Which enzyme catalyses this reaction?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: glutamate dehydrogenase performs oxidative deamination, using NAD+ or NADP+ and releasing NH4+.
distractorRationale.b: Glutamine synthetase adds ammonium to glutamate to make glutamine, using ATP; it releases no ammonium.
distractorRationale.c: ALT transfers an amino group to or from alanine and never produces free ammonium.
distractorRationale.d: AST also transfers amino groups without liberating ammonium.

questions.explanation: Only glutamate dehydrogenase liberates free ammonium from glutamate, by oxidative deamination coupled to NAD+ or NADP+ reduction. The aminotransferases merely shift amino groups. Glutamine synthetase works in the opposite direction, trapping ammonium.

questions.stem: True or false: transamination by an aminotransferase removes amino nitrogen from the body, because the amino group is released as free ammonium.
questions.explanation: Transamination only moves the amino group from one carbon skeleton to another, usually onto alpha-ketoglutarate to make glutamate. No ammonium is released at this step, so body nitrogen is unchanged. Free ammonium appears only when glutamate is deaminated by glutamate dehydrogenase.

questions.stem: In a patient fasting for 3 days, skeletal muscle exports 36 mmol of amino nitrogen to the liver over a period. One third of this nitrogen is carried as alanine and the remainder as glutamine. How many mmol of glutamine molecules were exported? (Alanine carries one nitrogen per molecule and glutamine carries two.)
questions.explanation: One third of 36 mmol N is 12 mmol N as alanine; the remaining 24 mmol N travels as glutamine. Since each glutamine carries 2 nitrogens, 24 divided by 2 gives 12 mmol glutamine. (Alanine would also be 12 mmol, since it carries one N each.)

questions.stem: Describe the role of pyridoxal phosphate in an aminotransferase reaction, using the conversion of alanine and alpha-ketoglutarate to pyruvate and glutamate as your example.
markingGuide: PLP is the active form of vitamin B6 and is bound to an active-site lysine as a Schiff base (internal aldimine)
Alanine displaces the lysine and forms a Schiff base with PLP; its amino group is transferred to PLP
Pyruvate is released and PLP is converted to pyridoxamine phosphate (PMP)
Alpha-ketoglutarate binds, accepts the amino group from PMP, and leaves as glutamate, regenerating PLP
PLP acts as an electron sink stabilising the intermediates; the sequence is a ping-pong mechanism
Net result: the amino group is transferred, not removed; reaction is reversible
questions.explanation: PLP is the carrier of the amino group within the enzyme: it accepts it from the first substrate (becoming PMP) and donates it to the second substrate (returning to PLP). The key points are the Schiff base chemistry, the PMP intermediate and the fact that the net reaction only moves nitrogen. A full answer links the mechanism to why B6 deficiency impairs transamination.

questions.stem: A woman is running an ultramarathon and her muscles are degrading some protein for fuel. Explain how the nitrogen and the carbon of the amino acids degraded in muscle reach the liver and what the liver does with each, naming the glucose-alanine cycle in your answer.
markingGuide: Amino groups are collected onto alpha-ketoglutarate by aminotransferases, giving glutamate
Glutamate transaminates with pyruvate (from glycolysis) via ALT to give alanine, which is exported to blood
Some glutamate is converted to glutamine by glutamine synthetase (ATP-dependent), carrying two nitrogens
In liver, ALT regenerates pyruvate and glutamate from alanine; glutaminase releases glutamate and NH4+ from glutamine
Glutamate dehydrogenase releases NH4+, which enters the urea cycle for disposal
Pyruvate is used for gluconeogenesis and glucose returns to muscle: the glucose-alanine cycle
Glucogenic carbon skeletons can provide glucose; ketogenic ones (leucine, lysine) cannot, going to acetyl-CoA and ketone bodies
questions.explanation: Muscle avoids releasing toxic free ammonium by passing nitrogen onto pyruvate (making alanine) and onto glutamate (making glutamine). The liver reverses both steps, sends NH4+ to the urea cycle, and uses the pyruvate for gluconeogenesis, completing the glucose-alanine cycle. The carbon skeletons are classified as glucogenic or ketogenic according to whether they give pyruvate and cycle intermediates or only acetyl-CoA and acetoacetate.

questions.stem: Isoleucine is degraded to succinyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA. How should isoleucine be classified?

options.text: Purely glucogenic, because succinyl-CoA is a citric acid cycle intermediate
Purely ketogenic, because acetyl-CoA is produced
Neither, because it is a branched-chain amino acid

distractorRationale.a: Correct: succinyl-CoA is glucogenic and acetyl-CoA is ketogenic, so both labels apply.
distractorRationale.b: This ignores the acetyl-CoA fragment, which is ketogenic.
distractorRationale.c: This ignores succinyl-CoA, which can be converted to oxaloacetate and glucose.
distractorRationale.d: Every amino acid carbon skeleton ends in a glucogenic or ketogenic product; being branched-chain does not exclude it.

questions.explanation: An amino acid is glucogenic if any of its carbon fragments can feed gluconeogenesis (succinyl-CoA qualifies) and ketogenic if any fragment becomes acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate (acetyl-CoA qualifies). Isoleucine gives one of each, so it is both.
